t: The Chamorro language belongs to the Malayo-Polynesian subgroup of the Austronesian family and took many Spanish loanwords in more than 300 years of Spanish rule.
During the Japanese occupation of Guam from 1941 to 1944, Chamorros were subjected to forced labour, imprisonment, torture and execution.
Chamorro institutions on Guam advocate the spelling CHamoru, which the language commission announced as the preferred standard in 2018.
dyk: In the Chamorro creation story the dying Puntan had his sister Fu’una make the world from his body: his eyes became the Sun and Moon and his eyebrows the rainbows.
ev: The ancestors of the Chamorro are commonly believed to have reached the Mariana Islands
Ferdinand Magellan’s ships reached the Marianas after crossing the Pacific
A Chamorro man and his friend killed the missionary Diego Luis de San Vitores and the catechist Pedro Calungsod
The United States captured Guam during the Spanish–American War
Japanese forces invaded Guam hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor
American forces recaptured Guam, a victory marked by Liberation Day
The Guam Organic Act made Guam an organised territory and its people US citizens
CHamoru was announced as the standard spelling of the people and language

f.homeland: The Mariana Islands, divided between the United States territory of Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, among them Guåhan (Guam), Luta (Rota) and Saipan; large communities also live in Hawaii, California, Washington, Texas and other US states
f.period: Arrival in the Marianas c. 1,500 BC; the Unai and Latte periods; Spanish rule 1521–1898; United States rule of Guam from 1898, with German and Japanese rule in the Northern Marianas; Japanese occupation of Guam 1941–1944; a living people today
f.known: the latte stone, now a national symbol; seafaring and outrigger canoes; weaving and pottery; the matrilineal clan; the creation story of Puntan and Fu’una; the value of inafa’maolek, “doing good for each other”; red rice and kelaguen
f.sources: Spanish colonial and missionary records (Charles Le Gobien, Pierre Coomans), the account of Christoph Carl Fernberger of 1623, archaeology, DNA studies of ancient remains, Chamorro oral tradition, and United States census figures
